tagline.text: An old southern Cebu town guarded by a coral-stone fortress church between mountain and sea

location.label: Location
location.text: Southeastern coast of Cebu Island, a small town about 103 km south of Cebu City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,500 (per person, based on a round-trip day trip from Cebu City including transport, meals and entrance fees)

children.text: Boljoon is a small town on the southeastern coast of Cebu, where a coral-stone fortress church from the late 18th century (Patrocinio de Maria church) is preserved as a national cultural treasure. It is a heritage town where you can walk to the old rectory museum, Spanish-era watchtowers and Ili Rock.

Boljoon is a coastal town about 103 km south of Cebu City. The 2024 census counted about 17,000 residents, and although it is small and quiet, it holds one of the best-preserved "fortress churches" in the Philippines, making it the heart of any southern Cebu history trip. The town's beginnings are dated to 1599, which makes it old even by Cebu standards; it became an independent vicariate on October 31, 1690, and passed to the Jesuits on September 27, 1737. It lies on the coastal road between Alcoy to the north and Oslob to the south, so it fits naturally into a trip down southern Cebu. It belongs to Cebu's "Heritage Frontier" of historic towns, and the town is small enough to explore on foot, a calm place to spend a day.

The center of any visit is the Church of Patrocinio de Maria Santisima (Boljoon Church). The first coral-stone church, built in the mid-18th century, was destroyed in a slave raid in 1782; rebuilding began the next year, and it is said to have been completed in 1814 under Fray Julian Bermejo. Its thick coral-stone walls and high windows were designed to serve as a refuge during Moro pirate raids, and the church grounds once had defensive structures and a perimeter wall. It was declared a National Historical Landmark in 1999 and a National Cultural Treasure in the early 2000s, and it is on UNESCO's tentative list under the "Baroque Churches of the Philippines (extension)." It also survived the 2013 Bohol earthquake without major damage. On April 23, 2022, the image of the Virgin received a canonical coronation. The church stands on a narrow coastal strip between mountain and sea, so walking into the churchyard you hear the sea on one side and see the mountain ridge on the other.

The old rectory (convento) beside the church is a Spanish-style stone house completed in 1847 and now serves as the parish museum. Its ground floor holds liturgical objects and artifacts excavated from the churchyard. In 2008 human remains and 16th-century artifacts were found in the churchyard, and in 2009 Japanese pottery turned up, which led to the interpretation that the town traded with Japan from the 16th century. The church cemetery keeps a coral-stone gate, traces of walls and bas-reliefs of skulls and crossbones, giving a feel of old times. Looking toward the sea from the plaza in front of the church, you can see where the old fort stood and the coastal road; even after the fort disappeared, the sight of the church standing between sea and mountain remained the town's symbol.

Walking around town, you will find four Spanish-era watchtowers (El Gran Baluarte, the tower on Ili Rock, Baluarte sa Fuente and the tower near Kayangon Point). El Gran Baluarte is the largest watchtower in Cebu province, and locals call it the "Kampanaryo" (bell tower). Their condition ranges from intact to ruins, so ask the town tourism office for their locations before you go. Ili Rock (Ilihan) rises near the shore, and from the top you can see the town and the sea at a glance. The whole town is a walkable size, and you can go around it following the Heritage Walk signboards.

A fortress-style church with thick coral-stone walls and high windows. About 90 percent of the 1782 structure remains, and inside you can see the choir loft and the old pipe organ (no longer played). The fort on the sea side was demolished in the 1900s when the coastal road was built.

This area keeps remains of the Spanish-era fortress structures, including a coral-stone gate and bas-reliefs of skulls and crossed bones. It is Boljoon's first Christian burial ground, made when the first stone church was built in the 1760s, and the ancestors of many local families are buried here. Walk through quietly.

The town has four watchtowers, and El Gran Baluarte is the largest. It was Fray Bermejo's headquarters, and its lower level is said to have served as a powder store and a jail. Ask the town tourism office about locations and whether you can approach them.
This rocky hill is visible even from the church plaza, and you can trek to the top for a view of the town. The route is not short, so ask a local for directions and watch for slippery rock.

The plaza across from the church is named after Fray Bermejo, and the parish complex also has the old Escuela Catolica (Catholic school). It is a good place for a slow walk and photos around the church.
The town's waters have several marine sanctuaries, including the Arbor Marine Sanctuary, which suit light snorkeling or sea-watching. Check locally how admission works and what it costs.
You can walk the whole town following signboards and get guidance from the municipal tourism office. A full loop takes about
2–3 hours

items.title: Day route
items.subtitle: Walking the church and watchtowers from Cebu City

children.text: Take a bus bound for Oslob or Santander from the Cebu South Bus Terminal in Cebu City.
Get off in Boljoon town and look around the plaza in front of the church, the church interior and the cemetery.
Visit the old rectory museum (check opening hours).
Have lunch at a town restaurant.
See the El Gran Baluarte watchtower and the view of Ili Rock.
Catch a bus back to Cebu City.
The bus ride takes about 3 hours and the last departure may be early, so leave some slack in the afternoon.

items.title: Overnight route
items.subtitle: A southern trip combined with Oslob

children.text: Head south from Cebu City and stop at towns along the way, such as Carcar.
Look around the church and museum in Boljoon.
See the town's sea and Ili Rock around sunset.
Move on to nearby Oslob and continue your plans.

The church, museum and plaza are within walking distance. For outlying watchtowers or beaches, use a tricycle or motorcycle taxi.
Boljoon has the tropical climate of southern Cebu. Because the visit centers on walking the town and climbing Ili Rock, the drier months are better.
In December there are many Masses around Christmas and the town gets busy; for a quiet visit, a weekday daytime is best.

Boljoon is a quiet rural town, and nights are still. There are small lodgings, homestays and beach resorts, but the choice is limited, so check the latest reviews on a booking site. Travelers usually make it a day trip from Cebu City or stay around Oslob or Moalboal and continue from there.

Food centers on Cebuano dishes at town restaurants and the market. Expect grilled fish and meat, rice and coconut drinks; no specialty dish has been confirmed. Some places stop serving early, so eat lunch early. According to some reviews, restaurants close early and the town is empty at night, so if you plan to stay until evening, check ahead for a hotel restaurant or simple snacks. Buying fruit and snacks at the town market and resting in the church's shade is also a modest, pleasant option.
The church is a place of worship, so keep quiet during Mass and dress with your shoulders and knees covered.
The museum may be closed on Mondays, so go during the hours reported as Tuesday to Sunday.
When getting off the bus, tell the conductor in advance that you want "Boljoon Church."
The plaza in front of the church has little shade, so bring a hat and water.
Ili Rock and the watchtowers have slippery rock, so wear shoes instead of sandals.
Ask at the tourism office for the Heritage Walk map and the watchtower locations.
If you are making a day trip, check the last bus back in advance.
Bring enough cash. ATMs are rare in the town.
Check whether photography is allowed inside the church, and do not disturb worshippers when photographing the altar.
The midday heat is strong between the church and the museum, so bring a hat and water bottle; photos in the morning or late afternoon make the coral-stone walls glow warmly in the sunlight.
Boljoon is a remote rural town, and late in the day there is almost no transport or food. For a day trip, leave before dark.
Bus fares and museum fees differ between sources, so check locally.
Some watchtowers are in ruins and the access paths may not be maintained, so take care.
Check waves and currents before swimming or snorkeling at sea, and only swim in safe spots.

Oslob
, to the south, is known for whale sharks and Sumilon Island tours, so it pairs well with Boljoon on a southern itinerary.
Sumilon Island
is a sandbar island reached by boat from Oslob.
